---
order: 4
unit: planning
title: Plan before you buy
node: AC9HE7K05 n4
summary: "A budget lists the money coming in and going out, so you can see what is left over, what you can afford, and how long saving for something will take, before you commit. Paying later still has an opportunity cost: each repayment is money you can't use for something else then. Knowing your rights and responsibilities is the other half of a good decision: check what you are agreeing to before you sign up."
language: maths
hook: "Sam wants a $240 bike. A sign says he can take it home today and pay later. Should he?"
---
Riverbend is a made-up town, and Sam's budget is made up.

A **budget** is a plan for your money: what comes **in**, what goes **out**, and what is **left over**. A **savings plan** uses what is left over to save for something over time.

A budget helps you decide **before** you commit: can you afford this, and how long will it take?

Some shops let you take something home now and **pay later** in parts. Paying later still has an opportunity cost: each repayment is money you can't use for something else then. Borrowing can be useful or costly, depending on what it's for. You'll look at that later.

## Predict: buy it today?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing first brings out the habit of deciding first and checking the money later."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Sam can take the $240 bike home today and pay $60 every two weeks. What should he do first?"
  options:
    - "Check his budget to see whether $60 every two weeks fits"
    - "Take it today: he'll work out the money later"
    - "Ask a friend what they think of the bike"
    - "Nothing: paying later means it costs nothing now"
  actual: "Checking the budget first shows whether the payments fit. Sam can then decide with his eyes open, and know what else he'll give up."
```

## Try: read Sam's budget

```step
stage: run
insight: "Reading a real-looking budget shows how the totals and the left-over amount are worked out."
try: { playground: board, starter: "budget.yml#run", height: 380 }
tasks:
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "How much does Sam spend each week (Total out)?"
      answer: 80
      explain: "$25 + $15 + $40 = $80, the formula in B9."
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "How much does Sam have left over each week?"
      answer: 30
      explain: "$110 in, $80 out, so $30 left over."
```

Click B11 and look at the bar above the sheet. It holds a formula, `=B4-B9`: total in, take away total out.

## Worked example: Nib's pay-later plan

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Nib's planted mistake is committing first and budgeting later. Writing the left-over formula is the move a budget needs."
try: { playground: board, starter: "budget.yml#investigate", height: 380 }
tasks:
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#nib"
      text: "Nib is giving Sam advice. Click the first line where Nib's thinking goes wrong."
      answer: 3
      fault: logic
      misconception: buy-then-budget
      explain: "Line 3: Sam should check his budget before he commits. He has $30 left over a week, which is $60 every two weeks: exactly the payment, with nothing spare. If a shift is cancelled, he could miss a payment, and missed payments can add fees. Line 4 hopes the money appears."
    smaller:
      check:
        type: number
        q: "Sam has $30 left over each week. How much is that every two weeks?"
        answer: 60
        explain: "$30 + $30 = $60, exactly one payment, with nothing spare."
  - check:
      type: board
      text: "B11 is empty. Write a formula in B11 that works out what Sam has left over."
      when: "f_B11 = 1 and c_B11 = 30"
      explain: "=B4-B9 takes the total out from the total in: $110 − $80 = $30."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "If Sam buys the bike on the pay-later deal, what is the opportunity cost?"
      options:
        - "What else he could have done with $60 every two weeks"
        - "Nothing, because he doesn't pay it all today"
        - "The whole $240, paid on the first day"
        - "Only the bike shop's costs"
      answer: 0
      feedback:
        - null
        - "Paying later still gives something up. It just happens later."
        - "He pays it in parts, not all on the first day. Each part is money he can't use for something else."
        - "The shop's costs aren't Sam's opportunity cost."
      explain: "Each repayment is money Sam can't spend or save for something else then. That is the opportunity cost of paying later."
```

### Find Nib's mistake

```worked
\text{In} :: $90 + $20 = $110 a week.
\text{Out} :: $25 + $15 + $40 = $80 a week.
\text{Left over} :: $110 − $80 = $30 a week, or $60 every two weeks.
\text{Pay-later deal} :: $60 every two weeks: all of it, with nothing spare.
\text{So} :: The budget shows the deal would use everything Sam has left. He should decide with that in view.
```

Now: where does Nib go wrong?

## Vary: change the plan

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Changing one line and watching the left-over amount update shows what a budget is for: trying a plan before you live it."
try: { playground: board, starter: "budget.yml#modify", height: 380 }
tasks:
  - check:
      type: board
      text: "Sam decides to spend less on food and going out. Change B8 to 25 and watch what is left over."
      when: "c_B8 = 25 and c_B11 = 45"
      explain: "Total out drops to $65, so Sam has $45 left over each week."
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "Saving $45 a week, how many weeks will it take Sam to save $240 for the bike? (Count a part week as a whole week.)"
      answer: 6
      explain: "$45 × 5 = $225, which isn't quite enough. After 6 weeks Sam has $270, enough for the bike."
```

## Practise: budgets and rights together

```step
stage: practise
insight: "A good decision uses both halves of the course: the budget and your rights and responsibilities."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Sam saves up and buys the bike. Which is his responsibility now?"
      options:
        - "Using the bike the way it's meant to be used"
        - "Getting a bike that is safe and works properly"
        - "Getting a refund if he changes his mind later"
        - "Getting a free warranty from the bike shop"
      answer: 0
      feedback:
        - null
        - "That's something Sam can claim: a right, under the consumer guarantees."
        - "The shop doesn't have to refund a change of mind."
        - "A warranty is something the shop may choose to give. It isn't Sam's responsibility."
      explain: "Using a product as it's meant to be used is the buyer's part: damage from misuse isn't covered by the guarantees. Keeping the receipt is a good habit too, though other proof of purchase also works."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Mia says: 'Budgets are only for people who are short of money.' What is the best reply?"
      options:
        - "Anyone can use a budget to see what they can afford and plan ahead"
        - "Mia is right: if you have enough, you don't need a plan"
        - "Budgets are only for businesses, not people"
        - "Budgets are only needed for things over $1000"
      answer: 0
      feedback:
        - null
        - "Even with plenty of money, a budget shows where it goes and helps you plan."
        - "People and businesses both use budgets."
        - "A budget helps with small decisions too, like Sam's bike."
      explain: "A budget is a tool for anyone who wants to plan, whatever the amount."
```

## Make: plan a purchase

```step
stage: make
insight: "Explaining how a budget and one right or responsibility would help someone decide is what this standard asks for."
try: { playground: board, starter: "budget.yml#make", height: 380 }
check:
  type: reasoning
  q: "Use the sheet to try a different plan for Sam (change what comes in or goes out). Then explain, in your book, how a budget helps Sam decide about the bike, and one right or responsibility he should know about before he buys."
  paper: true
  models:
    - title: "A strong answer"
      text: "The budget shows Sam has $30 left a week, so the pay-later payments would use all of it. If he cuts going out to $25, he can save the $240 in 6 weeks instead. Before he buys, he should know the bike must be of acceptable quality, and keep the receipt in case it isn't."
    - title: "A different plan that also works"
      text: "Sam could do two more lawns a week ($40 more), leaving $70 a week. Then the $60 payments every two weeks ($30 a week) would fit with $40 spare each week. He should still read the pay-later terms first, because that is his responsibility."
  criteria: ["I used the budget to show what Sam can afford.", "I said how long saving would take, or whether the payments fit.", "I named one right or responsibility."]
```

There is more than one good plan. Compare yours with the models, then talk it over with a partner.

## Typical: a business budget

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "Businesses budget too, and a savings plan helps them meet their responsibilities."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Riverbend Bakery puts $50 a week into a separate account for oven repairs. Why is that a good part of its budget?"
  options:
    - "If the oven breaks, it can fix it quickly and keep serving customers"
    - "So it never has to pay for anything else"
    - "Because the law says every bakery must save exactly $50 a week"
    - "So it can stop paying its staff"
  answer: 0
  feedback:
    - null
    - "The bakery still has other costs. This is one planned saving."
    - "No law sets that amount. It's the bakery's own plan."
    - "Paying staff is a responsibility. The savings plan is for repairs."
  explain: "A savings plan lets a business handle a known risk without stopping work."
```

## Wider: saving for a recall

```step
stage: make
tier: wider
insight: "A business that plans for problems is better placed to meet its responsibilities when something goes wrong."
check:
  type: question
  q: "A made-up toy maker keeps some money aside each year in case it has to run a recall. How does that connect to the last lesson?"
  options:
    - "It can pay to warn people and refund them if a toy is unsafe"
    - "It means the maker will never have to recall anything"
    - "It lets the maker skip the mandatory safety standards"
    - "It's spare profit the owners can take out at year's end"
  answer: 0
  feedback:
    - null
    - "Saving doesn't stop problems happening. It helps the maker respond."
    - "Mandatory standards still apply, whatever the maker saves."
    - "Money set aside for recalls isn't paid out as profit."
  explain: "Budgeting for possible recalls helps a business meet its responsibility to customers when a product turns out to be unsafe."
```

Typical and wider steps are extras on the same idea. You do not need them to finish the lesson.

```teacher
summary: "Students explain how a budget and savings plan support better
  decisions about consumer and financial products, using a made-up weekly budget
  on a small spreadsheet, and link the decision to a right or responsibility.
  The planted mistake is committing to a pay-later deal first and budgeting
  afterwards. Debt is touched, not taught: paying later still has an opportunity
  cost, and borrowing can be useful or costly depending on what it's for."
learning: explain how a budget or savings plan supports a decision about a
  purchase, and link it to a consumer right or responsibility
time: 45
timing: Predict and Try 8 min · Worked example 14 min · Vary 8 min · Practise 6
  min · Make 9 min. Typical and wider steps are extras and not counted in this.
goals:
  - I can read a budget and work out what is left over.
  - I can write a formula for what is left over, and change the plan to see what
    happens.
  - I can explain why checking a budget before committing helps, including with
    pay-later deals.
  - I can link a purchase decision to one right or responsibility.
struggle: "Students treat the budget as something you do after you've bought.
  Ask: what would the budget have told Sam before he signed?"
before: >
  **Debt is a touch, not a lesson (Matthew, 1 Nov 2026).** Buy-now-pay-later is
  real and students see it in ads, so it is named by type (never by brand). Year
  7's job is checking that repayments fit the budget before committing (this
  node), and seeing that paying later still has an opportunity cost. Whether a
  particular debt is worth it, interest, and good and bad debt are later work:
  business borrowing in AC9HE8K05, good and bad debt in AC9HE9K01, short- and
  long-term costs of loans in AC9HE10K03. Student text says borrowing "can be
  useful or costly, depending on what it's for. You'll look at that later." If
  students ask, an example of useful borrowing: a business borrowing for a
  machine that lets it do more work than the repayments cost. That comparison is
  for the later standards.


  **Facts about buy-now-pay-later (checked 1 Nov 2026):** from 10 June 2025,
  buy-now-pay-later contracts come under Australia's credit laws, and providers
  need a credit licence (ASIC media release 25-069MR). The lesson only says that
  missed payments "can add fees", which is true of many such deals; it doesn't
  state any provider's fees.


  **Privacy and care.** Nothing asks about students' own money, pocket money or
  family spending. Families use credit, including pay-later, for many reasons;
  nothing in the lesson judges them. Budgeting is one useful habit, not a moral
  test, and not every household can save the same way.


  Sam's budget and the bike are made up; the amounts are invented for easy
  arithmetic, not real prices.


  The sheet is the ICT course's `sheet` board: students click a cell and type; a
  formula starts with `=`. If students haven't met spreadsheets, show B4
  (=SUM(B2:B3)) first.
running:
  - "Predict: take a vote. Many will say 'take it today'."
  - "Try: put the sheet up and read it together; click B11 to show the formula."
  - "Worked example: ask 'How much does Sam have every two weeks?' before
    revealing Nib's mistake. Then students write the formula in B11."
  - "Vary: students change B8 and watch B11. Ask what else Sam could change
    instead."
  - "Make: students try their own plan on the sheet, then explain it in their
    book."
stuck:
  - see: A student says paying later costs nothing now, so there's no cost.
    ask: Where does the $60 every two weeks come from?
    fix: Each repayment is money you can't use for something else then. That's the
      opportunity cost of paying later.
  - see: A student types 30 in B11 instead of a formula.
    ask: If Sam's bakery pay changes, will 30 change too?
    fix: A formula like =B4-B9 keeps the answer right when the numbers change.
  - see: A student says debt is always bad.
    ask: Could borrowing ever help someone do more than it costs them?
    fix: Borrowing can be useful or costly, depending on what it's for. That's for
      later years; here, the habit is checking it fits first.
stretch: Sam's bakery shifts are casual, so some weeks he gets fewer. How would
  you change the budget to plan for a slow week? It does not go on to another
  lesson.
support: "A three-line card: In − Out = Left over. Then: Left over × weeks ≥ price?"
leads: >
  This is the last lesson in Consumer rights and responsibilities. The
  spreadsheet skills come from ICT › Working with data, if students want more
  practice.


  Wider (teacher choice, not part of the student steps): the node's wider items
  include how access to budgeting and financial tools differs across
  communities, including remote and First Nations communities. If you take this
  up, use local, community-approved material and First Nations-led sources. The
  lesson writes nothing about it.
exit:
  q: How does a budget help before buying something on a pay-later deal? Name one
    right or responsibility that also matters.
  a: "The budget shows what is left over, so you can check the repayments fit and
    see what else you'd give up. Rights: the product must be of acceptable
    quality. Responsibilities: read the terms, use the product as it is meant to
    be used. (Keeping the receipt is a good habit.)"
explain: >
  A **budget** shows money **in**, money **out**, and what is **left over**. A
  **savings plan** uses what is left over to save over time. Checking the budget
  **before** committing shows whether you can afford it and how long saving will
  take.


  Paying later still has an opportunity cost: each repayment is money you can't
  use for something else then. Borrowing can be useful or costly, depending on
  what it's for.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Sam can take a $240 bike home today and pay $60 every two weeks. What would
      you want to know before saying yes?
    prompts:
      - Where would the $60 come from?
      - What would Sam not be able to do with that money?
    notes: Collect questions; most of them are answered by a budget. Talk about Sam,
      not students' own money.
  activities:
    - at: run
      kind: activity
      title: Read the budget together
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Put Sam's sheet up. Ask the class to find total in, total out and what
        is left over, then click B11 to show the formula.
      notes: If the class hasn't used spreadsheets, show B4's =SUM first.
    - at: modify
      kind: discussion
      title: Try a plan
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Change one line on the board live (food and going out, or an extra
        lawn). Ask how many weeks the bike takes now.
      notes: "Each change is a choice with its own opportunity cost: less going out,
        or more work."
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Every two weeks
      type: question
      q: Sam has $30 left over each week. A pay-later deal asks for $60 every two
        weeks. What does the budget show?
      options:
        - It would use everything Sam has left, with nothing spare
        - He would have $30 spare every two weeks
        - He can't afford any of it
        - The deal costs nothing
      answer: 0
      explain: $30 × 2 = $60, exactly the payment. A cancelled shift could mean a
        missed payment.
```
